summary.text:
York publishes more operational detail than almost anyone: every loan repaid, every loan drawn, the rate and duration of each. Sixteen new loans totalling £87.80m, fifteen of them PWLB at 4.31% to 4.80% over one to five and a half years.

The strategy shift is documented and honest. All of 2024/25's borrowing was one-year PWLB. During 2025/26 they moved deliberately into the 1-6 year range because those rates 'were on average below 5%, typically offering the best value' — and then reverted to one-year maturities in March 2026 when the Middle East conflict spiked the curve. The consequence is stated: £53.75m matures in 2026/27, £32.80m of it drawn this year on a year or less.

They also cleared their last LOBO. The lender gave notice in September 2025 that it would raise the rate at the 1 October option date on a £5m loan running nominally to 2077; York declined and repaid in full. The portfolio now holds none. Against a CFR of £514.83m and total external debt of £400.30m, internal borrowing is £114.53m. Two officer addresses are published, and their report carries MUFG's dated rate forecast, which is now five months old and testable.

officer.subject: Your March forecast, five months on
officer.body:
Hi Debbie,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts ahead of Executive on 9 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

Your annual report is one of the most operationally transparent we've read — every loan repaid and every loan drawn, with the rate and the duration. Sixteen new loans, £87.80m, and you can see the thinking change across the year in the maturities.

That thinking is the reason I'm writing. All of 2024/25's borrowing was one-year PWLB. Through 2025/26 you moved deliberately into the 1-6 year range because those rates were "on average below 5%, typically offering the best value", and then reverted to one-year maturities in March when the Middle East conflict spiked the curve. Paragraph 54 states the consequence plainly: £53.75m matures in 2026/27, £32.80m of it drawn this year on a year or less.

So the question of where rates go next lands on you sooner than on most. Your Table 1 carries MUFG's forecast dated 25 March, which put September 2026 certainty rates at 5.00% for five years, 5.50% for ten, 6.00% for twenty-five and 5.80% for fifty. Our series for today gives 5.34%, 5.83%, 6.46% and 6.27% — between 0.33 and 0.47 above the forecast, five months on. Bank Rate at 3.75% the forecast got right; the curve it didn't. That's not a criticism of the forecast, it's the argument for watching the actual daily rather than the projection quarterly, which is what pwlbtoday.org/dashboard is for.

The other thing worth saying is that clearing the last LOBO looks like a good call in hindsight. The lender gave notice in September, you declined the new rate and repaid £5m on a loan nominally running to 2077. You're now one of very few councils we've read holding none at all — Kent, Newcastle, Tameside and Bath & North East Somerset all still have live options, and Dexia has called at two of them this year. That's a pattern only visible if you read everybody's papers, which is what we do.

We hold your PWLB loans and price them daily against the DMO's repayment curve, so premium and discount positions are a page rather than a piece of work: pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. We never present it as a quote; the DMO's is the binding one. The monthly sector breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%, so you can see how much appetite there is before you need it.

On training, three fit York: Strategic PWLB borrowing, given the 2026/27 concentration; Interest rate risk; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data and worth a look with the Prudential and Treasury Codes under review. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the scrutiny your Audit and Governance Committee gives this. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
